newsitem.title: UK: Delays seen in Cuban sugar shipments, offers scarce.
newsitem.headline: Delays seen in Cuban sugar shipments, offers scarce.

text.p: Cash prices for Cuban raw sugar are remaining stable at a large discount to New York futures but offers are thin on the ground, physical sugar brokers said on Thursday.

The exact situation regarding Cuban availability is somewhat unclear but market sources said an apparent supply hiccup meant that even holders of Cuban contracts were having to wait until about April for their sugar.
"There are problems with the Cuban crop so there is less available than was anticipated earlier," said one trader.
"What was there has now been sold and everything else is trading because nobody can trade Cubans."

Other traders said Cuba had cut back on some of its obligations due to the lateness of the crop and also because the island's cane had not properly recovered from the damaging effects of Hurrican Lili, which swept over western and central Cuba last October.
Officials said at the time that although areas of cane had been flattened or flooded most of it would still be useable.
London traders quoted February cargoes at a discount of around 50 points to New York futures and broadly the same level for further forward deliveries.

But regional supply is also tighter than usual due to the absence of north Brazilian raws from the market, with Brazilian millers even paying to buy back their own cargoes to fulfil their U.S. quota allocation.
Some major trade houses are believed to hold large amounts of Mexican raws and the trade is generally long of physical sugar in the region, market sources said.
"A lot of the supply has been taken out -- the big difference this year is that there are no north Brazils spare," said one broker.
The fluctuations of the whites premium, affecting millers' willingness to undertake tolling operations, and the falling Thai raw premium would also affect the raws supply, brokers said.

In its latest biweekly report, broker Merrill Lynch said tolling operations could step up if raw futures were to slide quickly again, which would be supportive for the New York market if the white premium remained firm.
"The decision by EU producers to carry over slightly more sugar than previously planned has helped to keep the whites premium steady," the Commodity Market Trends report said.
But Cuba will have to compete with falling Thai prices, especially for its exports into Asia which more than doubled in 1996.
In its daily report, statistician F.O. Licht said Cuba was Asia's largest raws supplier last year with 1.155 million tonnes after 515,000 tonnes in 1995.
"I would expect the (Cuban) discount to gradually erode. But if Thai premiums come down to around 16 (points) or so, then it's difficult for the Cubans to improve much," the broker said.
Thai premiums were quoted earlier this week at 25/30 points bid/offer over New York futures for March/May shipment, compared with around 40/45 a month ago.
Iran and Venezuela have both been buyers of Cuban raws over the past two weeks.
Venezuela, where refining margins are said to be relatively cheap, is said to have imported 150,000 tonnes of Cuban raws and thus reached maximum tolling capacity.

Russia is believed to be importing Cuban raws but much of this sugar is likely to be destined for former Soviet republics such as Kazakhstan where local prices are higher than on the well-stocked Russian market.
